opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different layers to this, and I'd separate the skills question from the working-methods question, because they interact in interesting ways.

On the skills side, the first thing I'd emphasize is that evaluating scheming is, at its core, an empirical science problem that happens to be very young. So the most valuable skill is something like good experimental taste: being able to look at a vague, scary concept, like "the model is pursuing a hidden goal and strategically deceiving its overseers," and break it down into components you can actually measure. Does the model have situational awareness? Does it understand that it's being evaluated? Can it reason about its own incentives? Will it take covert actions when given an opportunity? Each of those can become a concrete eval, and the craft is in designing environments where the behavior you're looking for can show up, while ruling out the boring alternative explanations.

That second part is really important. A lot of the time, when you see something that looks like scheming, the real explanation is something mundane. The model was confused by the instructions, or the prompt practically told it what to do, or it's role-playing because the scenario looks like a fiction setup. So I think a strong researcher in this area needs a kind of adversarial skepticism toward their own results. You want to be the first person to try to explain your finding away. If it survives that, then you have something.

The second skill is just being very hands-on with models. I think people underestimate how much you learn from reading a lot of transcripts. Not summary statistics, actually reading what the model wrote, especially the reasoning traces when you have access to them. You develop intuitions about when the model is genuinely reasoning about its situation versus pattern-matching. That intuition is hard to get any other way, and it's what lets you design the next experiment well.

Third, solid engineering. A lot of this work is building realistic agentic environments: sandboxes, tools, fake codebases, fake company emails, whatever the scenario needs. Realism matters a lot, because increasingly models can tell when something looks like a test. So the ability to build environments quickly and make them convincing is a real bottleneck, and people who are good engineers with research sensibility are extremely valuable.

On working methods, a few things I believe pretty strongly. One is fast iteration loops. Early on, you want to go from idea to "did anything interesting happen?" in hours or days, not months. Most ideas don't pan out, and you want to find that out cheaply. Then, once something looks real, you slow down and get much more rigorous: more samples, ablations, controls, varying the prompts to check robustness.

Another is being explicit about what claim you're making. There's a big difference between "models are capable of this kind of deception when strongly nudged" and "models do this spontaneously in realistic deployment." Both are useful findings, but they have very different implications, and I think the field gets into trouble when those get conflated, either in the direction of hype or in the direction of dismissal.

And then a broader point: I think the field needs to think about evaluation awareness as a first-class problem. As models get more capable, the naive approach of "put the model in a scenario and see what it does" becomes less reliable, because the model may recognize the scenario and behave differently. So methods that don't rely purely on behavior, like looking at reasoning traces, interpretability-style approaches, or monitoring in real deployment, become more important over time. A good researcher here should be thinking not just about today's eval, but about how it will break as models improve.

So if I had to summarize: empirical taste, deep skepticism of your own results, lots of direct contact with model behavior, strong engineering, and a clear sense of exactly what your evidence does and doesn't show.

r001.rationale: It calls strong engineering a bottleneck for building realistic environments, but does not say that limited software engineering skills become a bottleneck after initial progress.

r002.rationale: It says researchers should break the concept of scheming into measurable components and design experiments that distinguish the behavior from alternative explanations.

r003.rationale: It recommends reading model transcripts, especially reasoning traces, and says that this direct exposure helps researchers design the next experiment.

r004.rationale: It advocates fast iteration loops, but does not identify them as the main driver of progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a fairly weird mix of skills, and that's part of what makes it hard to hire for.

The first thing I'd say is that it's much more empirical than people expect. When we started Apollo, I think I had this picture that a lot of the work would be conceptual — sitting down and thinking really hard about what deceptive alignment looks like in theory, and then deriving evals from that. And some of that is useful. But in practice, most of the progress has come from just sitting with the model for hours, running it through scenarios, reading transcripts, noticing something slightly odd, and then poking at it. A lot of our best findings started as "huh, that's weird" rather than as a clean hypothesis.

So I'd say the single most important skill is something like scientific taste combined with a willingness to get your hands dirty. You need to be able to look at a transcript where the model does something that looks like sandbagging or disabling oversight and ask: is this actually the thing I care about, or is this an artefact of the prompt? Did I accidentally tell it to do this? Would a reasonable person reading this say the model was scheming, or am I pattern-matching too eagerly? That kind of scepticism towards your own results is really crucial, because the failure mode in this field is very much crying wolf. If you publish three results that turn out to be prompt artefacts, nobody will listen when you find the real thing.

The second skill is just good engineering. The evaluation infrastructure matters a lot more than I initially appreciated. You want to be able to run a scenario across many models, many variations of the prompt, many seeds, and then actually look at the distribution rather than cherry-picking one dramatic transcript. That requires building tooling that lets you iterate fast. So a lot of the team's time is honestly closer to software engineering than to research in the traditional sense.

Then there's a third thing, which is harder to name, but it's something like red-teaming intuition or adversarial thinking. You're trying to construct situations where, if the model had certain goals or dispositions, those would show up in its behaviour. That means you have to think from the model's perspective: what would it need to believe about its situation for this to be a real test? Does it think it's being evaluated? Does it have a plausible reason to behave badly here? If the scenario is too contrived, the model either refuses or treats it as a game, and you learn nothing.

And then related to that, you need to be quite careful about the difference between capability and propensity. Can the model scheme if you push it to, versus does it scheme on its own when it has some goal that conflicts with its developers'? Those are different questions, they need different experimental designs, and conflating them is one of the most common mistakes I see.

On working methods — I think the thing that's served us best is a kind of fast loop between qualitative and quantitative. You read transcripts until you have a hunch, you design a controlled version, you run it at scale, you look at the numbers, and then you go back and read transcripts again because the numbers always hide something. People who only do the quantitative part tend to miss what's going on, and people who only read transcripts tend to overfit to vivid examples.

And the last thing I'd say is that it helps enormously to have people on the team who are a bit paranoid and people who are a bit sceptical, and to let them argue. Internally we try to have someone whose job in a given project is basically to say "I don't buy it" and try to explain the result away. If the result survives that, it's probably worth publishing.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering and evaluation infrastructure matter, but does not say limited engineering skills become a bottleneck after initial progress.

r002.rationale: It calls conceptual work useful and emphasizes judging whether results reflect real scheming, but does not state that conceptual understanding is needed to determine which measurements are meaningful.

r003.rationale: It describes reading transcripts and revising controlled scenarios, but does not mention inspecting models’ chains of thought in evaluation rollouts.

r004.rationale: It says most progress has come from empirical testing and identifies a fast loop of transcript review, controlled experiments, scaled runs, and renewed transcript review as the approach that has served best.

astra-6.text:
I think you need a combination of good empirical research skills and a fairly adversarial mindset. You’re trying to understand what a model can do, but you’re also asking whether the way you’re testing it would actually reveal the behaviour you care about. If a model recognises that it’s being evaluated, or if your setup makes scheming very unlikely, then getting a reassuring result doesn’t necessarily tell you very much.

A lot of the work is turning a vague concern into something you can investigate. What would the model need to understand about its situation? What opportunities would it have to act deceptively? What would count as evidence that it was doing that, rather than just misunderstanding the task? You need to make those distinctions concrete enough that you can build experiments around them.

And then there’s a lot of iteration. You run an experiment, look closely at what happened, find that some part of your setup wasn’t testing what you thought it was testing, and improve it. Good engineering matters because it lets you do that quickly, but so does being willing to read individual examples and notice unexpected behaviour.

I’d also emphasise being sceptical in both directions. You shouldn’t take a model saying something sinister as proof of scheming, and you shouldn’t take the absence of obvious scheming as proof of safety. The useful skill is figuring out what your evidence actually supports, and what experiment would most reduce the remaining uncertainty.

r001.rationale: It says good engineering helps researchers iterate quickly, but does not state that limited software engineering skills become a bottleneck after initial progress.

r002.rationale: It explains that researchers need to make the concern concrete, distinguish scheming from misunderstanding, and identify what would count as evidence before building experiments.

r003.rationale: It mentions reading individual examples and noticing unexpected behavior, but does not describe inspecting chains of thought in evaluation rollouts to revise evaluations.

r004.rationale: It describes iterative experiments and improvements, but does not identify rapid empirical feedback loops as the main driver of progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it requires a combination of being quite rigorous and being quite creative. The creative part is asking: if a model were scheming, what might that look like? In what situations would it have an incentive to hide what it’s doing? And how could we construct a test where we’d actually notice that?

But then you need the rigor to distinguish scheming from something much more mundane. Maybe the model misunderstood the task. Maybe your prompt essentially told it to behave deceptively. Maybe there’s an issue with the evaluation setup. A suspicious-looking transcript is a starting point for an investigation; you need follow-up experiments to understand what caused the behavior.

So the working method I’d emphasize is a fairly fast experimental loop. Build a simple test, look closely at what the model actually does, form hypotheses, and then change the setup to distinguish between those hypotheses. That involves engineering, but also a lot of judgment about what an experiment does and doesn’t establish.

And I think it helps to be comfortable having your initial interpretation turn out to be wrong. You want to take the possibility of scheming seriously while being very willing to discover that a particular result has another explanation. The goal is to understand the model well enough that the evidence is useful for decisions.

r001.rationale: The response mentions engineering, but does not say limited software engineering skills become a bottleneck after initial progress.

r002.rationale: It discusses imagining scheming and judging experiments, but does not state that conceptual understanding is needed to determine which measurements are meaningful.

r003.rationale: It says to inspect what the model does, but does not describe inspecting chains of thought in evaluation rollouts or using them to revise evaluations.

r004.rationale: It identifies a fast experimental loop—build a test, inspect behavior, form hypotheses, and adjust the setup—as the working method it emphasizes for evaluating scheming.
